sentences.text: Heptasuchus was a medium-sized rauisuchian with a skull measuring about 65 centimeters in length and an estimated total body length between 4.9 and 5.2 meters.

Although no complete skull is known, preserved elements suggest it was similar to the German taxon Batrachotomus, featuring an arched nasal bone, a large naris, and a postorbital bar entering the eye orbit.
Reconstructions of this animal depict unusually large premaxillary teeth, a feature based on a single premaxillary tooth that was partially erupted from its socket.
The skeleton possessed a long, straight pubis curved anteriorly with a pubic boot, and a slender ulna lacking the strong olecranon process seen in Postosuchus.
Its hind limb anatomy included a long, straight pubis that was curved in anterior view and featured a pubic boot.
Heptasuchus was formally described and named by Robert M. Dawley, John M. Zawiskie, and J. W. Cosgriff in 1979, with Heptasuchus clarki as the type species.
The generic name Heptasuchus combines the Greek word for 'seven' and the Latinized name of the Ancient Egyptian crocodile god Sobek.
The specific name 'clarki' honors George Clark of Casper, who discovered the type locality.
The holotype consists of a partial skull and partial postcranial skeleton (UW 11562), while paratypes include unassociated partial cranial and postcranial remains (UW 11563 to UW 11565).
Most Heptasuchus specimens were thought to be lost until 1997, when it was confirmed they reside at the University of Wyoming, though some elements remain missing.
Heptasuchus was a hypercarnivore that likely hunted or scavenged other animals in its environment.
This hypercarnivore likely hunted or scavenged on other animals within its ecosystem.
Aggregations of Heptasuchus may indicate that these hypercarnivores dominated dwindling water supplies during droughts before succumbing to the conditions themselves.
The fossil locality likely represents a drought assemblage, evidenced by weathered, disarticulated specimens confined to a small area.
Heptasuchus was originally assigned to the family Rauisuchidae based on shared traits with genera such as Prestosuchus, Postosuchus, and Saurosuchus.
Zawiskie et al. (2011) diagnosed Heptasuchus using two autapomorphies: large, posterodirect flanges on the parabasisphenoid and a distinctive postfrontal projecting from the orbit.
Phylogenetic analyses suggest Heptasuchus is the sister taxon to Batrachotomus within the clade Loricata, supported by at least six shared character states.
A phylogenetic analysis suggested Heptasuchus and Batrachotomus are sister taxa within the group Loricata, supported by at least six shared discrete character states.
The Paleobiology Database lists Heptasuchus as belonging to the parent group Poposauridae.
Heptasuchus lived during the Carnian stage, approximately 237 to 227.3 million years ago.
The type locality dates to the Carnian or late Ladinian, based on its lithostratigraphic position below the lower part of the Popo Agie Formation.
Heptasuchus likely lived during the Carnian or late Ladinian stages of the Triassic, though the exact age is not precisely known.
It was once hypothesized that Heptasuchus might be synonymous with Poposaurus, but this hypothesis has since been refuted.
It is debated whether Heptasuchus was an obligate quadruped or a facultative biped.

It is debated whether all pseudosuchian elements from the locality belong to Heptasuchus; while Wroblewski (1997) suggested the taxon was a paleontological chimera, Zawiskie et al. (2011) argued it is not.
